text.tspan: 115 laps at Thunderhill West across five track days,
logged on two apps that disagree with each other.
The interesting part wasn't building the chart. It was
redesigning it a year later and finding what I'd let
slide because I already knew the answer.
Each mark is one lap. The heavy line under each track day is that day's
— my fastest sectors, strung together. The floor: pace
I'd already proven in pieces but hadn't put in one lap.
The gap between floor and cluster is the honest measure. Not "am I
faster?" — that flatters you, because tyres and weather and traffic all
move. It's "how close am I to the lap I've already proven?"

Reviewing my own chart a year later
The original is still on Tableau Public. A serviceable chart; I was pleased
with it. Coming back cold, I could see where I'd designed for someone
who already knew the answer — which is to say, for me.
A teal dot and a purple dot, unlabelled. I knew which
was which. Nobody else did. Now they say
Marks the size of the story
Large opaque circles buried the early sessions in one
blob. Smaller marks with some transparency let density
Callouts drew rules straight through the plot. Detail
now sits in a readout below, so nothing is drawn over
It read 95s, 100s, 105s. Nobody at a track day talks
, and the x-axis is split by track
day instead of an unlabelled run.
None of it is dramatic. That's the point — it's the ordinary maintenance
a chart needs when it stops being something you made and becomes
I only caught it by treating my own work
as though someone else submitted it.
1:39 to 1:28.39 — eleven seconds over a season, almost none of it
in one leap. The theoretical-best floor drops steadily, and the cluster
follows at a lag. I could always drive the sectors before I could drive
The wet session is the most useful thing here, and I nearly filtered it out
for being ugly. Forty seconds of penalty on the same day I set my best
time argues about context better than any dry lap could.
wasn't noise. It was the finding.
